The first: that it is the equality of night and day; this is what Wahb ibn Munabbih said.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 73, verse 19–20:

﴿And Allah determines the night and the day.﴾ That is, He determines their hours. This may have two meanings:

One: His determining them for the deeds of His servants.

Two: For His decree concerning His creation.

﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it.﴾ On this there are two views:

One: You will not be able to bear the night prayer (qiyam al-layl). This is the view of al-Hasan.

Two: He means the determining of half the night, its third, and its quarter. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

﴿So He has turned to you in forgiveness.﴾ This may have two meanings:

One: He has forgiven you for your shortcomings in the past, so recite in the future what is easy.

Two: He has lightened [the obligation] for you.

﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an.﴾ On this there are two views:

One: Pray what is easy of the prayer. He has expressed the prayer by the Qur'an because the prayer includes Qur'an recitation.

On this view, regarding what is meant by "what is easy of the prayer," two meanings are possible:

One: That which is performed voluntarily as supererogatory prayer (nawafil), because an obligatory fixed prayer is not one for which one is commanded to do "what is easy."

Two: That it refers to the obligatory prayers of the five daily prayers, since people transition from the night prayer to them, and the phrase "what is easy" is to be understood as relating to the manner of performance in strength and weakness, health and sickness, and not as relating to a number prescribed by the law.

Two: That this means the recitation of what is easy of the Qur'an, taking the address according to the apparent wording.

On this view there are two meanings:

One: That it means reciting the Qur'an within the prayer, so the command to it is obligatory, since recitation in the prayer is obligatory.

There is disagreement about the amount of it that one must recite in the prayer. Malik and al-Shafi'i determined it to be the Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha); it is not permissible to deviate from it or to limit oneself to part of it. Abu Hanifa determined it to be a single verse from whatever part of the Qur'an it may be.

The second view: that it means reciting the Qur'an outside the prayer. On this view, is the unqualified command of this kind to be understood as obligatory or recommended? On two views:

One: That it is to be understood as obligatory, so that one may stand before its miraculous nature through its recitation, and the proofs of monotheism and the sending of the messengers in it. He is not required, once he has recited it and recognized its miraculous nature and the proofs of monotheism from it, to memorize it, because memorizing the Qur'an is among the recommended acts of worship, not the obligatory ones.

Two: That it is to be understood as recommended rather than obligatory. This is the view of the majority, because if it were obligatory for him to recite it, it would be obligatory for him to memorize it.

Concerning the amount of recitation included in this command, there are five sayings: First: the whole Qur'an, because Allah the Exalted has made it easy for His servants. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Second: a third of the Qur'an, related by Juwaybir.

Third: two hundred verses, said by al-Suddi.

Fourth: one hundred verses, said by Ibn Abbas.

Fifth: three verses, like the shortest surah, said by Abu Khalid al-Kinani.

﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill.﴾ Allah mentioned the causes of lightening, and among them He mentioned illness, because it incapacitates.

Then He said: ﴿And others travel through the land﴾. On this there are two meanings:

One: That they are the travelers, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And when you travel through the land, there is no blame on you for shortening the prayer﴾.

Two: That it is moving about for trade, based on His saying: ﴿seeking of the bounty of Allah﴾, said by Ibn Mas'ud, traced to the Prophet, and it is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿And others fight in the way of Allah﴾, meaning in His obedience, and they are the strivers (mujahidun).

﴿So recite what is easy of it.﴾ It abrogated what He had made obligatory at the beginning of the surah concerning the night prayer, and made what is easy of it voluntary and supererogatory, because an obligation is not one for which one is commanded to do "what is easy" of it.

We have mentioned at the beginning of the surah the sayings concerning the duration of the obligation.

﴿And establish the prayer﴾, meaning the obligatory one, which is the five at their times.

﴿And give zakah﴾. On this there are three sayings: First: that here it means obedience to Allah and sincerity to Him, said by Ibn Abbas.

Second: that it is the zakat al-fitr, said by al-Harith al-Ukli.

Third: that it is the zakah on all wealth, said by Qatadah and Ikrimah.

﴿And lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾. On this there are five interpretations: First: that it means the supererogatory acts after the obligatory ones, said by Ibn Zayd.

Second: the saying "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest," said by Ibn Hibban.

Third: spending on one's family, said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

Fourth: spending in the way of Allah, and this is the view of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

Fifth: that He commanded the performance of all acts of obedience for which one deserves reward.

﴿You will find it with Allah﴾, meaning you will find its reward with Allah. ﴿It is better﴾, meaning than what you gave and did.

﴿And greater in reward.﴾ Abu Hurayrah said: Paradise.

It may also be that "greater in reward" means the giving of ten for one good deed.

﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah﴾, meaning for your sins.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ of what came before repentance.

﴿Merciful﴾ to you after it, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.
